afghanistan.context: its public calendar combines Islamic observances with civic dates, while Nowruz remains a familiar spring-season reference in parts of Afghan cultural life
afghanistan.language: Dari and Pashto are widely used, alongside other community languages; ask which language feels natural to the recipient.

occasions.name: Nowruz
occasions.when: Around the March equinox, usually in March.
occasions.detail: Nowruz marks the arrival of spring and is observed culturally by some Afghan communities, even though official recognition and public practice can differ. Its family and renewal associations make it a useful seasonal reference, but it should not be described as universal or as a single standard event across the country.

occasions.name: Eid al-Fitr
occasions.when: At the end of Ramadan, on the first day of Shawwal in the Islamic lunar calendar.
occasions.detail: For Muslim families who observe Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr follows a month of fasting and prayer. It is commonly associated with Eid prayers, visits and sharing food or gifts with relatives. The local date depends on the relevant moon-sighting announcement, so avoid scheduling a first-day greeting from a fixed Gregorian date.

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.when: On 19 August, marking the 1919 independence agreement.
occasions.detail: Afghanistan’s Independence Day is a civic anniversary connected with the country’s recovery of control over its foreign affairs. Public commemorations and private feelings about national history can be complex. A personal note can acknowledge the day while wishing safety, dignity and a peaceful future rather than assuming one political viewpoint.

sensitivities: Do not assume that every Afghan observes Nowruz in the same way; the occasion has varied cultural and political visibility.
Religious greetings should be sent to people whose observance you know, not inferred from a name or nationality.
National history and current politics are sensitive subjects; keep a personal greeting humane and non-partisan.

albania.context: the calendar includes both civic anniversaries and spring observances such as Summer Day and Nevruz, alongside Christian and Muslim holidays
albania.language: Albanian is the national language, while family and diaspora preferences may include other languages; use the language you share.

occasions.name: Summer Day (Dita e Verës)
occasions.when: On 14 March, with celebrations especially associated with central Albania and Elbasan.
occasions.detail: Summer Day welcomes the coming of spring and has a strong association with Elbasan, where traditional sweets and public festivities are part of the occasion. Its recognition has spread nationally, but the way families mark it varies. A greeting about brighter days and seasonal renewal fits better than claiming every household follows one ritual.

occasions.name: Nevruz
occasions.when: Around 21 March, at the spring equinox.
occasions.detail: Nevruz is observed by Bektashi communities and also appears in Albania’s public holiday calendar. It is connected with renewal and the arrival of spring. A respectful message can recognise the season and the recipient’s community, without treating a religious-cultural observance as a practice shared by all Albanians.

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.when: On 28 November, with Liberation Day following on 29 November.
occasions.detail: The November national days recall Albania’s declaration of independence and the country’s liberation history. The flag and national symbols are visible in civic celebrations, and the dates may carry strong family or diaspora meaning. Keep a wish warm and respectful rather than turning it into a political statement.

sensitivities: Albania has Muslim, Catholic, Orthodox and non-religious communities; do not assume a person’s faith.
Nevruz is particularly meaningful within Bektashi tradition, so name it carefully rather than treating it as everyone’s religious holiday.
Historical and political interpretations can differ; a simple wish for the country’s wellbeing is usually safer than a debate.

algeria.context: the annual calendar brings together Amazigh and Arab heritage, national liberation commemorations and Islamic dates that move through the solar year
algeria.language: Arabic and Tamazight are official languages; French is also used in some settings, so follow the recipient’s preference.

occasions.name: Yennayer (Amazigh New Year)
occasions.detail: Yennayer marks the Amazigh New Year and is a recognised cultural occasion in Algeria. Family meals, regional foods and cultural events may accompany the day, with practices differing between Amazigh communities and households. A greeting that acknowledges Amazigh heritage is more accurate than presenting one regional dish or custom as universal.
occasions.theme: a generous and hopeful new year

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.detail: Independence Day recalls the end of French colonial rule after a long and costly struggle. Official ceremonies and family remembrance can give the day a serious as well as celebratory tone. A personal greeting can wish peace, dignity and opportunity while recognising the historical importance of the date.

occasions.name: Revolution Day
occasions.when: On 1 November, marking the start of the liberation struggle in 1954.
occasions.detail: The 1 November commemoration honours the beginning of the Algerian War of Independence. It is a national remembrance date, not simply a festive break. Choose language that respects sacrifice and family memory, and avoid casual jokes or language that trivialises the history.

sensitivities: Algeria’s Arabic-speaking, Amazigh and other communities are not culturally interchangeable; do not reduce the country to one language or identity.
Revolution-related dates refer to a painful anti-colonial history and deserve a respectful tone.
Islamic holiday dates follow the lunar calendar and local announcements; verify timing before sending a time-specific greeting.

andorra.context: local life mixes Catalan-language traditions with the principality’s civic calendar and Christian feast days
andorra.language: Catalan is the official language; Spanish, French and Portuguese may also be used in everyday life, so do not guess the recipient’s preference.

occasions.name: Constitution Day
occasions.detail: Constitution Day marks the approval of Andorra’s modern constitution and is a civic moment for the principality. It is often quieter than a large cultural festival. A greeting that wishes the recipient and the country stability, wellbeing and a positive year ahead is appropriate without overdoing patriotic language.

occasions.name: Sant Jordi (Saint George’s Day)
occasions.when: On 23 April, in the Catalan cultural calendar.
occasions.detail: Sant Jordi is associated with books, roses and the exchange of thoughtful gifts in Catalan-speaking settings. In Andorra it offers a distinctly cultural way to send a personal note, particularly to someone who enjoys reading. Do not assume every household follows the same gift custom; a message about stories and affection can stand alone.

occasions.name: Our Lady of Meritxell Day
occasions.detail: Meritxell Day honours the country’s patron saint and has both religious and national significance. For some residents it is a family or faith occasion; others relate to it primarily as a public holiday. Let the recipient’s own relationship to the celebration guide how explicitly religious your greeting should be.

sensitivities: Andorra’s public culture is Catalan, but residents use several languages; avoid assuming Spanish is everyone’s first choice.
Meritxell is a Catholic devotion, not a universal religious observance.
Small local festivals and parish celebrations can be community-specific; avoid describing them as nationwide customs without evidence.

angola.context: the calendar includes national liberation and peace commemorations, Carnival and Christian dates, with strong regional variation in music and community celebrations
angola.language: Portuguese is the official language, while many Angolans also use national languages; use the recipient’s comfortable language.

occasions.name: Carnival
occasions.when: Usually in February or March, before Lent.
occasions.detail: Angolan Carnival is linked to music, dance and public performance, with Luanda among the best-known centres. Groups and neighbourhoods may prepare costumes and performances, while other people enjoy the holiday more quietly. A greeting can celebrate creativity and shared energy without assuming that everyone attends a parade.

occasions.name: Peace and Reconciliation Day
occasions.detail: This civic date marks the 2002 peace agreement that ended Angola’s civil war. Its meaning is more reflective than a party greeting: it can be a moment to wish stability, rebuilding and a peaceful future. Avoid language that minimises the suffering of people affected by the conflict.

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.detail: Independence Day recalls Angola’s end of Portuguese colonial rule. Public ceremonies and cultural programming may feature national symbols and music. For someone with family connections across the country or abroad, a message about belonging and hope can feel personal without assuming a particular political view.

sensitivities: The civil-war period is part of living family memory; do not trivialise the Peace and Reconciliation commemoration.
Portuguese is widely used but does not represent every home language or local identity.
Carnival styles and participation vary by city and community; avoid treating Luanda’s programme as the entire country.

antigua-and-barbuda.context: the twin-island calendar centres on Carnival, national independence and community events that connect residents with Caribbean heritage
antigua-and-barbuda.language: English is the official language and Antiguan Creole is common in everyday conversation; mirror the recipient’s own style.

occasions.name: Antigua Carnival
occasions.when: Usually from late July into the first week of August.
occasions.detail: The summer Carnival period brings calypso, soca, steel-pan music, mas bands and community events. Its schedule spans several days and is especially significant on Antigua; Barbuda’s community life has its own rhythms. A personal note can celebrate creativity and togetherness without assuming everyone attends the street events.

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.detail: The anniversary marks independence in 1981 and is often accompanied by official ceremonies, cultural programmes and national pride. A greeting can recognise the country’s history and wish continued opportunity for both islands. Avoid treating the two islands as culturally identical or implying that every resident joins public celebrations.

occasions.name: Christmas
occasions.when: On 25 December, during the Caribbean dry-season period.
occasions.detail: Christmas is observed by many Christian households through worship, family visits and seasonal food, while practice differs across the islands and families. Keep a message personal rather than assuming a particular church tradition. For a recipient away from home, a wish for connection and rest can be especially meaningful.

sensitivities: Carnival is a public cultural celebration, but attendance and preferred styles differ by person and island.
Use the recipient’s preferred name for Antigua, Barbuda or the wider nation rather than assuming one island identity.
Religious greetings should reflect the person’s own observance, not their nationality alone.

argentina.context: the civic year includes May Revolution and Independence commemorations, while Carnival and regional traditions add local colour
argentina.language: Spanish is the main shared language, but regional expressions and forms of address vary; write in the register you already use with the person.

occasions.name: May Revolution Day
occasions.detail: The May Revolution commemorates the events of 1810 that began the process leading to independence. It is a national civic date, often marked with ceremonies and public gatherings. A greeting can recognise history and shared identity without claiming that everyone relates to the anniversary in the same way.

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.detail: Argentina’s Independence Day recalls the declaration made in Tucumán in 1816. The date often carries school, civic and family significance, and is especially meaningful to people who have moved abroad. A warm message can connect the historical anniversary with hopes for the recipient’s future.

occasions.name: Day of Tradition
occasions.detail: The Día de la Tradición honours the country’s gaucho heritage and literary figure José Hernández. It can be marked through folk music, dance, food and regional events. Because traditions differ widely across Argentina, focus on the recipient’s own connection rather than using gaucho imagery as a national stereotype.

sensitivities: Argentina’s regions and communities are diverse; gaucho culture is important but does not define every person.
Civic history can be politically charged; keep celebratory messages respectful rather than partisan.
Do not assume a recipient drinks mate, follows football or identifies with a single regional custom.

armenia.context: the year features Armenian Apostolic Christmas, spring civic anniversaries and Vardavar, a summer festival with ancient roots
armenia.language: Armenian is the national language; Russian and other languages may be used in some families and diaspora settings, so follow the recipient’s preference.

occasions.name: Armenian Christmas
occasions.when: On 6 January in the Armenian Apostolic tradition.
occasions.detail: The Armenian Apostolic Church celebrates the Nativity and Epiphany together on 6 January. Families may attend church services and share meals, while the day can be deeply meaningful to Armenian communities abroad. A warm wish can refer to peace, family and faith without assuming that every Armenian is Apostolic or religious.

occasions.name: Vardavar
occasions.when: Usually in July, 14 weeks after Easter in the Armenian Church calendar.
occasions.detail: Vardavar is a summer festival associated with water-splashing traditions and the Transfiguration feast. Public play can be lively, but participation is a personal choice and the observance also has religious meaning. A greeting about summer joy and renewal is suitable without encouraging unwanted splashing or treating consent as optional.

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.detail: Armenia’s Independence Day commemorates the 1991 independence referendum. It is a civic occasion that can carry strong meanings for people in Armenia and across the diaspora. A note wishing security, peace and opportunity is thoughtful, especially given the region’s difficult recent history.

sensitivities: Armenian Christmas follows a different date from many Western Christmas calendars; use 6 January for the Apostolic tradition.
Vardavar is not permission to throw water at someone who does not want to participate.
Conflict, displacement and genocide memory are sensitive subjects; do not use them as casual greeting themes.

australia.context: the year combines national civic dates with remembrance, seasonal holidays and community observances that reflect a highly diverse society
australia.language: English is the common public language, but many households use other languages; mirror the recipient’s own choice.

occasions.name: Australia Day
occasions.detail: Australia Day is the national day, but it is also contested by many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people as Invasion Day or Survival Day. The date can therefore carry different meanings within the same family or workplace. Before sending a patriotic greeting, consider the recipient’s perspective; a neutral wish for wellbeing avoids assuming agreement.

occasions.name: ANZAC Day
occasions.detail: ANZAC Day commemorates Australians and New Zealanders who served and died in wars and conflicts. Dawn services, marches and quiet remembrance are central to the day. It is a solemn commemoration rather than a conventional celebration, so use language of respect, gratitude and remembrance rather than party-style congratulations.

occasions.name: Christmas
occasions.when: On 25 December, during the Australian summer.
occasions.detail: Christmas is marked by Christian worship and by secular family gatherings, often during summer holidays. Outdoor meals and travel are common possibilities, but weather and household practice differ across the continent. A greeting can be warm and seasonal without assuming a religious observance or a particular family arrangement.

sensitivities: Australia Day is not experienced as celebratory by everyone, especially many First Nations people; do not assume a patriotic message is welcome.
ANZAC Day is a remembrance occasion; avoid jokes or promotional language.
Australia’s climate and regional seasons differ; do not assume a snowy Christmas or one shared outdoor tradition.

austria.context: the calendar is shaped by Catholic and wider Christian observances, regional customs, and the modern republic’s October national day
austria.language: German is the main language, with regional varieties and many family languages; choose the form of address the recipient normally uses.

occasions.name: National Day
occasions.detail: Austria’s National Day marks the 1955 declaration of permanent neutrality and is associated with the republic’s modern constitutional identity. Public institutions may hold open days and ceremonies. A personal greeting can wish the recipient a peaceful holiday and a positive future without turning neutrality into a political debate.

occasions.name: Advent and Christmas
occasions.when: Throughout December, with Christmas Eve on 24 December and Christmas Day on 25 December.
occasions.detail: Advent markets, seasonal music and family preparations are visible in many parts of Austria, while Christmas observance differs between religious and secular households. The main family gathering may take place on Christmas Eve. A considerate greeting can wish calm and time with loved ones rather than assuming a specific church practice.
occasions.theme: calm and time with loved ones

occasions.name: Easter
occasions.when: In March or April, following the Christian calendar.
occasions.detail: Easter is an important Christian season in Austria, with church services, family meals and regional customs. The exact date changes each year. Some people mark the religious meaning, while others treat the holiday as a family break. A wish focused on peace and renewal works across those differences.

sensitivities: Catholic traditions are prominent in some Austrian regions but do not describe every resident.
Regional holidays and customs differ between the federal states; do not call one local practice nationwide.
Use formal German address when appropriate, particularly with older people or in professional relationships.

azerbaijan.context: Novruz is a major spring celebration, alongside national independence and modern state commemorations
azerbaijan.language: Azerbaijani is the state language; Russian and other languages may be used in some communities, so mirror the recipient.

occasions.name: Novruz
occasions.when: Around 20–21 March, at the spring equinox; public celebrations span several days.
occasions.detail: Novruz is a major cultural holiday associated with spring, renewal and heritage. Families may prepare traditional foods, visit relatives and mark the days before the equinox with customs that vary by household and region. A wish can mention fresh beginnings and abundance without presenting every folk practice as compulsory.

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.detail: Independence Day commemorates the 1918 establishment of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic. Public ceremonies and national symbols give the date a civic character. For a personal greeting, a wish for peace, prosperity and opportunity is appropriate; avoid assuming the recipient shares a particular political outlook.

occasions.name: Victory Day
occasions.detail: Victory Day is a major national commemoration connected with the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war. It can be deeply emotional for families and veterans. A respectful note should avoid triumphalist language about suffering and should not reopen conflict debates; wishes for peace and safety are more considerate.

sensitivities: Novruz is shared across several cultures, but local customs and preferred spellings can differ.
The Nagorno-Karabakh conflict and displacement remain sensitive; do not use celebratory language that dismisses loss.
Religious Eid dates are set by the lunar calendar and official announcements, not a fixed Gregorian date.

bahamas.context: Junkanoo is a distinctive parade tradition, while Independence Day and Emancipation-related dates add civic and historical meaning
bahamas.language: English is the official language; Bahamian English and Creole expressions may appear in familiar speech, so follow the recipient’s style.

occasions.name: Junkanoo
occasions.when: Most prominently on Boxing Day and New Year’s morning, with other seasonal events in some islands.
occasions.detail: Junkanoo features elaborate costumes, handcrafted groups, music and street parades, especially in Nassau and on several Out Islands. Preparation can take months, so it is more than a one-day spectacle. A personal wish can recognise the creativity and community work behind the celebration, not just the parade itself.

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.detail: The Bahamas became independent in 1973, and the July anniversary is marked with ceremonies and public events. The country’s many islands have distinct local identities, so a greeting may be more meaningful when it acknowledges the recipient’s home island or family roots rather than treating the archipelago as one uniform place.

occasions.name: Emancipation Day
occasions.when: On the first Monday in August, depending on the annual public holiday arrangement.
occasions.detail: Emancipation observances connect the present with the history of slavery and freedom in the Caribbean. For a personal message, use thoughtful language about dignity, memory and community. Avoid reducing the day to a summer party or assuming every family marks it through the same event.

sensitivities: Junkanoo has historical roots connected to enslaved Africans; do not treat it as costume entertainment without cultural context.
The Out Islands have their own identities and events; not every celebration is Nassau-centred.
Emancipation is a serious historical commemoration as well as a public holiday.

bahrain.context: the calendar includes Islamic lunar observances, Ashura and national days, with communities observing religious occasions in different ways
bahrain.language: Arabic is the official language and English is common in many settings; use the language already shared with the recipient.

occasions.name: Eid al-Fitr
occasions.when: At the beginning of Shawwal, immediately after Ramadan.
occasions.detail: Eid al-Fitr follows Ramadan and may involve early prayers, family visits and shared meals. The public holiday period is announced according to the lunar calendar. occasions.name: Ashura
occasions.when: On the tenth day of Muharram in the Islamic lunar calendar.
occasions.detail: Ashura has particular religious significance for Shia Muslims and is marked in Bahrain through commemorations and processions in some communities. occasions.name: National Day
occasions.when: On 16 December, with related national celebrations around the date.
occasions.detail: Bahrain’s National Day is a civic occasion associated with the country’s modern history and leadership. Public decorations and events may accompany the holiday. Bahrain includes Sunni, Shia, Christian and other communities; do not assume a person’s faith.

barbados.context: Crop Over, Emancipation Day and Independence Day form a seasonal sequence tied to the island’s music, agricultural and historical heritage
barbados.language: English is official, while Bajan speech is part of everyday cultural life; avoid imitating dialect unless it is natural between you.

occasions.name: Crop Over
occasions.when: Usually across the summer, culminating in Grand Kadooment in early August.
occasions.detail: Crop Over developed from the end-of-sugar-cane-harvest celebrations and now includes calypso, soca, arts events and a large costumed parade. occasions.name: Emancipation Day
occasions.detail: Emancipation Day marks the abolition of slavery in Barbados and is closely connected with the island’s history and cultural identity. It may sit alongside Crop Over events, but its meaning is not simply carnival. A message about dignity, memory and freedom is more appropriate than a generic party greeting.

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.detail: Independence Day marks Barbados becoming independent in 1966. Civic events and cultural programmes may take place, and the season can also carry personal meaning for Barbadians overseas. A greeting that wishes continued wellbeing and opportunity is warm without needing to make political claims.

sensitivities: Crop Over’s history includes plantation labour and emancipation; do not erase that context.

belarus.context: the year includes Independence Day, Victory Day and midsummer Kupalle, while Orthodox and Catholic calendars both influence family life
belarus.language: Belarusian and Russian are widely used; ask which one the recipient prefers rather than guessing from location.

occasions.name: Victory Day
occasions.detail: Victory Day commemorates the end of the Second World War in Europe and carries strong remembrance associations in Belarus. Families may remember relatives who served or suffered during the war. A respectful greeting can acknowledge memory and wish peace, rather than treating the date as a casual party.

occasions.name: Kupalle (Midsummer)
occasions.when: Around the summer solstice, commonly on the night of 6–7 July.
occasions.detail: Kupalle is a traditional midsummer celebration associated with folk songs, fire, water and seasonal rituals. Modern events can blend local heritage with public entertainment, but customs vary by region and family. A greeting about summer, nature and cultural continuity is more fitting than claiming every household performs the same ritual.

occasions.name: Independence Day

occasions.detail: Belarus marks Independence Day on 3 July, a date tied to the Second World War history of the capital. The anniversary has both civic and historical layers. occasions.name: Belgian National Day
occasions.detail: Belgium’s National Day commemorates the oath of the first king in 1831. Ceremonies, concerts and public events take place in the capital and elsewhere. The country is organised around Dutch-, French- and German-speaking communities, so a greeting in the recipient’s own language is more thoughtful than assuming one language fits all.

occasions.name: Saint Nicholas (Sinterklaas)
occasions.when: Around 6 December, especially in Flemish-speaking communities and family settings.
occasions.detail: Saint Nicholas is a children’s gift-giving tradition in parts of Belgium, with local variations in timing and customs. occasions.name: Christmas and Easter
occasions.when: Christmas on 25 December; Easter follows the Christian calendar in March or April.
occasions.detail: Christian calendars remain visible in Belgium’s public holidays, but family practice ranges from religious services to secular gatherings. belize.context: national civic dates sit alongside Maya, Garifuna, Creole and other community traditions, including the November Garifuna Settlement Day observance
belize.language: English is official, while Kriol, Spanish, Garifuna and Maya languages are part of community life; ask what feels familiar.

occasions.name: National Day (St George’s Caye Day)
occasions.detail: The September commemoration recalls the Battle of St George’s Caye and is part of Belize’s national civic calendar. It is followed by Independence Day later in the month, creating a distinctive patriotic season. A greeting can wish the recipient pride and a peaceful future without assuming one historical interpretation.

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.detail: Belize marks independence from Britain in 1981 with parades, cultural performances and national symbols. The country’s multilingual communities give the season a varied character. A personal note can recognise Belizean identity while making space for the recipient’s own town, language and family traditions.

The observance belongs especially to Garifuna heritage; name that community rather than treating it as a universal custom.

benin.context: Vodun heritage, national independence and the country’s varied Christian and Muslim observances all appear in the public calendar
benin.language: French is official, while Fon, Yoruba and many other languages are spoken; use the language you share with the recipient.

occasions.name: Vodun Days
occasions.when: In January, centred on Ouidah; the national traditional-religions holiday is set for the second Friday of January.
occasions.detail: Vodun Days present the arts, ceremony and spiritual heritage associated with Vodun, especially in Ouidah. A greeting should recognise the tradition with respect and avoid using sacred imagery as decoration.

occasions.name: Independence Day
occasions.detail: Benin’s Independence Day commemorates independence from France in 1960. Civic ceremonies and public gatherings may mark the anniversary. A personal message can wish the recipient and the country peace, opportunity and confidence, without making assumptions about political views or how publicly someone celebrates.

occasions.name: Gaani
